content: Patients should be monitored for signs of adverse effects related to BCRP substrates, and the dosage of these substrates should be adjusted according to their product labeling. Ethinyl estradiol and valoctocogene roxaparvovec both increase the risk of interactions with other medications, necessitating careful monitoring. Medications that may cause hepatotoxicity when combined with valoctocogene roxaparvovec can elevate the risk of liver enzyme abnormalities, so these combinations should be closely monitored, and alternative therapies considered if drug interactions are likely. Ethinyl estradiol can decrease the levels or effects of valproic acid by increasing its elimination, potentially leading to an increased frequency of seizures. Therapy should be modified, and patients monitored closely. Voriconazole can increase the levels or effects of ethinyl estradiol by affecting hepatic and intestinal CYP3A4 metabolism, requiring caution and close monitoring. Levonorgestrel transdermal systems may enhance the effects of warfarin through an unspecified interaction mechanism, necessitating careful observation. Adverse effects associated with these medications include weight gain, cholelithiasis, cholecystitis, major depression, suicidal ideation, appendicitis, ectopic pregnancy, pneumonia, and gastroenteritis. Women experiencing headaches with focal neurological symptoms, migraines with aura, or those over 35 years old with any type of migraine should avoid these medications. Women with a BMI ≥30 kg/m² may experience reduced contraceptive effectiveness and a higher risk of venous thromboembolism (VTE) compared to those with lower BMI. These medications are contraindicated in individuals with liver tumors (benign or malignant), acute viral hepatitis, severe cirrhosis, or other liver diseases. They should not be used in cases of undiagnosed abnormal uterine bleeding, pregnancy, or a history of breast cancer or other estrogenor progestin-sensitive cancers. Hypersensitivity to any components of these medications, including reactions such as itching or irritation at the application site, is also a contraindication. The use of hepatitis C drug combinations containing ombitasvir, paritaprevir, ritonavir (with or without dasabuvir) is contraindicated due to the potential for elevated ALT levels. Women taking ethinyl estradiol-containing medications with these hepatitis C regimens have shown increased ALT levels. These medications are also contraindicated in women with uncontrolled hypertension or hypertension with vascular disease. Age-related cardiovascular risk factors, such as hypertension, diabetes, dyslipidemia, and obesity, should be considered when prescribing these medications. Combination hormonal contraceptives (CHCs) may increase the risk of gallbladder disease. They are contraindicated in diabetic women aged 35 years or older, or in women with diabetes complicated by hypertension, nephropathy, retinopathy, neuropathy, vascular disease, or diabetes of more than 20 years' duration. Women with a history of depression should be carefully observed, and the medication discontinued if depression becomes severe. CHCs are associated with an increased risk of cervical cancer or intraepithelial neoplasia, though it is unclear whether this is due to the medication itself or other factors such as sexual behavior. Estrogen may increase serum concentrations of thyroxine-binding globulin, sex hormone-binding globulin, and cortisol-binding globulin, potentially requiring adjustments in thyroid hormone or cortisol replacement therapy. Exogenous estrogens may induce or exacerbate symptoms of angioedema. CHCs should be discontinued if pregnancy occurs. Contraceptive hormones and/or their metabolites are present in human milk and may reduce milk production in breastfeeding women, though this is less likely once breastfeeding is well established. Breastfeeding women should be advised to use alternative contraceptive methods until breastfeeding is discontinued. Ethinyl estradiol reduces the release of luteinizing hormone-releasing hormone (LHRH) from the hypothalamus and gonadotropin release from the pituitary, while increasing DNA, RNA, and protein synthesis in target tissues. It may also alter cervical mucus to inhibit sperm penetration and induce endometrial changes that reduce the likelihood of implantation. Levonorgestrel transdermal systems inhibit ovulation through a negative feedback mechanism on the hypothalamus, reducing follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinizing hormone (LH) secretion. Since it is applied transdermally, first-pass metabolism via the gastrointestinal tract or liver is avoided. These medications should be stored in their original pouch until application and kept at room temperature (20–25°C or 68–77°F), with permissible excursions to 15–30°C (59–86°F).
